meta.description: Yes — genuinely Nietzsche. It's from Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883), “On the Poets.” The popular one-liner is a condensed paraphrase of the real sentence.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They muddy the waters to make them look deep'?
meta.ogDescription: A real Nietzsche line from Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883), “On the Poets” — but the familiar wording is a smoothed paraphrase, not a canonical translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Nietzsche line. In Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Part II, “On the Poets,” 1883) Zarathustra says of poets, “they all muddy their water so that it may seem deep” (German: sie trüben alle ihr Gewässer, daß es tief scheine). The familiar one-liner “They muddy the water, to make it seem deep” is a smoothed, condensed English rendering rather than a word-for-word canonical translation.

source.excerpt: They are also not pure enough for me: they all muddle their water that it may seem deep. And fain would they thereby prove themselves reconcilers: but mediaries and mixers are they unto me, and half-and-half, and impure!
trail: The genuine sentence appears in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Part II, “On the Poets,” where Zarathustra complains that poets “all muddle their water that it may seem deep” ↗ (Common, 1909).
The German original of 1883 reads “sie trüben alle ihr Gewässer, daß es tief scheine” ↗ — literally “they all muddy their waters, so that it may seem deep.”
Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced section for Thus Spoke Zarathustra ↗, quoting Kaufmann’s “they all disturb their waters so that they may seem deep.”
The condensed pop-culture wording “They muddy the water, to make it seem deep” is the form spread by quote sites and social media — a faithful paraphrase, not a verbatim published translation.
source.excerptNote: Thomas Common’s 1909 translation. The German original reads: “Sie sind mir auch nicht reinlich genug: sie trüben alle ihr Gewässer, daß es tief scheine.” Kaufmann (1954) renders it “they all disturb their waters so that they may seem deep.”

source.rightsNote: The German text was first published in 1883 and Thomas Common’s English translation in 1909 — both well before 1931, so both are in the public domain in the United States. (Later translations such as Kaufmann’s 1954 version remain in copyright, but the underlying line and the pre-1931 renderings are free to use.)

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher, cultural critic and classical philologist whose work on morality, nihilism and the “will to power” reshaped modern thought. Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883–1885), written in a mock-biblical, aphoristic style, is his best-known book and a favourite mine for quotable lines — which is exactly why paraphrased and fabricated “Nietzsche” quotes circulate so widely.

misattribution.heading: About the wording
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Nietzsche is correct — the thought and the source are genuinely his. What’s off is the exact wording: the version that circulates online is a condensed paraphrase, not a line from any standard published translation.

items.why: The widely-shared “They muddy the water, to make it seem deep” does not match any canonical translation verbatim. Nietzsche’s sentence in context is longer and more pointed — Common renders it “they all muddle their water that it may seem deep” ↗.

Many copies swap in “waters…deep” or “make them look deep.” In Nietzsche the poets muddy their water so that it (the water, i.e. their own depth) seems deep — the target is the poets’ self-presentation, per the sourced Wikiquote passage ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: really Nietzsche, really from Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883) — but the crisp one-liner is a modern condensation of his actual sentence, “sie trüben alle ihr Gewässer, daß es tief scheine” ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The image comes from Zarathustra’s attack on poets in Part II of Thus Spoke Zarathustra. Nietzsche — himself a poet-philosopher — accuses poets of faking profundity: stir up the water, make it cloudy, and shallow ideas can pass for deep ones. It is a self-implicating jab, since Zarathustra admits “I am of to-day and heretofore… but there is something in me that is of to-morrow.”
detailsBody: In the chapter, Zarathustra says poets “have not thought deeply enough” and so “their feeling itself has not gone down to the depths.” The muddied-water metaphor is the punchline of that complaint — obscurity mistaken for depth.

Because the line is so aphoristic, it detached from its context and became a general-purpose jab at pretentious experts, academics and jargon — usually in the smoothed form “muddy the water(s) to make it/them seem/look deep.”
